crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Satellite Imagery
children.blurb: Satellite imagery as alternative data refers to the use of overhead optical, radar, and multispectral images to measure economic activity that is not captured in standard financial statements or government releases.

children.name: Card Transaction Data
children.blurb: Card transaction data refers to aggregated and anonymized records of purchases made with credit, debit, and prepaid cards, used by economists and analysts to track consumer spending, revenue trends, and regional economic activity.

children.name: Sensor and Shipping Data
children.blurb: Sensor and shipping data as alternative data covers physical-world signals from vessel transponders, port sensors, weather stations and cargo telemetry, used to estimate trade flows, commodity supply, congestion and industrial activity.

children.name: Mobile Location Data
children.blurb: Mobile location data refers to aggregated or individual-level geospatial records collected from smartphones and other connected devices, used as an alternative dataset for economic analysis, retail footfall, mobility, and real estate.

children.name: Web Data Collection
children.blurb: Web data collection in alternative data means gathering publicly available information from websites, forums, job boards, app stores, social media, and regulatory filings to build datasets that supplement traditional financial and economic data.

sections.body: Alternative data is information not from standard financial statements or official statistics, such as satellite images, card spending records, sensor feeds, shipping manifests, mobile location pings, and public web pages. AI is used to turn these raw, messy sources into signals: computer vision counts cars in parking lots or oil storage tanks, natural language processing reads job postings and reviews, and anomaly detection flags changes in shipping traffic. In practice, funds, retailers, insurers, and logistics firms use these signals to estimate revenue, supply chain stress, foot traffic, and consumer demand before quarterly reports appear. The work is not magic; it is a pipeline of collection, cleaning, entity matching, and modeling. The AI Economist section treats alternative data as an economic input, not just a technical curiosity. That framing matters because the value comes from a decision that someone makes with the signal.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature. Satellite imagery for crop yields, parking lot counts, and oil tank shadows has been used for years, and card transaction panels are a standard input for nowcasting consumer spending. Sensor and shipping data are well established in logistics, where telematics and port records feed routing and inventory models. Mobile location data and web data collection are more contested, because consent, privacy law, and platform terms change quickly. The honest limits are coverage bias, panel drift, identity resolution errors, and the fact that a correlation between a satellite image and a company's revenue can break when operations change. The site's 146 active AI lawsuits and 215 compliance and regulation pages reflect how often collection methods face legal challenge, and no model fixes a bad sample or turns a noisy proxy into ground truth.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section divide the field by source and by the problems each source creates. Satellite Imagery covers overhead sensing, computer vision for object detection, and the gap between a pixel and a financial estimate. Card Transaction Data deals with panel construction, spend categorization, and the difficulty of separating a company's sales from broader consumer shifts. Sensor and Shipping Data looks at telemetry, port calls, container flows, and the operational use of real time tracking. Mobile Location Data addresses foot traffic, visit attribution, and the privacy questions that make this source legally fragile, while Web Data Collection covers scraping, public records, job postings, and the legal and technical limits of gathering information from the open web. A reader can move from one page to another to compare how each source is collected, what AI does with it, and where the evidence is strong or weak.
